Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 1:

(p-154) Surat an-Najm (The Star)

﴿By the star when it sets﴾. The meaning of "the star" (al-najm) is either al-Thurayya (the Pleiades), for it is the name predominantly applied to it, or the category of stars in general, and its "hawiy" (setting, falling) is its going down. It has also been said that it refers to its rising. One says: "hawa hawiyyan" on the pattern of qabula (to set, to go down) when it sets, and "hawiyyan" on the pattern of dakhula (to rise, to ascend) when it rises and mounts. As for the star of the stars of the Qur'an (najm min nujum al-Qur'an), its "hawiy" is its descent (nuzul). The governing element (al-'amil) of "idha" is the verb of the oath, by this, for it carries the sense of unrestricted time, detached from the meaning of the future, as in your saying: "I will come to you when the unripe dates turn red." In swearing by this, to affirm the purity of him (ﷺ) from any trace of misguidance and error, there is an eloquent originality and a beauty of placement beyond which there is no further limit. As for the first two interpretations, it is because the star's nature is that the traveler by night is guided by it along the paths of the world, as if it were said: "By the star by which the wayfarers are guided to the right path."

﴿Your companion has not strayed﴾, i.e., he has not deviated from the path of truth, which is the way to the Hereafter.

﴿Nor has he erred﴾, i.e., he has never believed in falsehood. He is in the utmost state of guidance and rectitude, and he is in no way what you imagine of misguidance and error at all. As for the third interpretation, it is an honouring of the status of the Qur'an, as was alluded to at the beginning of Surah Ya Sin and Surah al-Zukhruf, and an indication of the basis of his (ﷺ) guidance and the source of his rectitude. It is as if it were said: the Qur'an, which is a sign in guidance to the paths of the religion and the ways of truth, Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) has not strayed from it, nor has he erred. The address is to Quraysh, and the mention of him (peace and blessings be upon him) by the title of their companion is both to point out that they knew the details of his noble conditions and were thoroughly acquainted with his innocence of what is completely denied of him, and with his (peace and blessings be upon him) possession of the utmost guidance and rectitude. For their long companionship with him (peace and blessings be upon him) and their witnessing of his great excellent qualities necessarily requires this. The restriction of the oath to the time of his descent (hawiyy) in the last interpretation is evident. As for the first two interpretations, the star is not one by which the traveller is guided when it is in the middle of the sky, nor can the east be known from the west, nor the north from the south by it; rather, one is guided by it when it sets or rises. Along with this, there is perfect suitability in it for what will be related about Jibril (Gabriel) descending from the highest horizon and drawing near to him, peace be upon them both. This is what befits the dignity of the noble revelation. As for interpreting his descent (hawiyy) as its scattering on the Day of Resurrection, or as the shooting of the star by which devils are pelted, or interpreting the star as the plant, and interpreting its descent as its falling to the earth, or (p-155) as its emerging from it, these are not suitable to the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 3:

﴿And he does not speak from [his own] desire﴾ That is: his speech of the Qur'an does not issue from his whim or opinion at all. For what is intended is the continuity of the negation of speech from desire, not the negation of the continuity of speech from it, as has passed many times.

Translation:

﴿It is not﴾, i.e., what he utters of the Qur'an.

﴿except a revelation﴾ from Allah, exalted is He. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that is revealed﴾ is a descriptive qualifier emphasizing "revelation," removing the possibility of metaphor (majaz) and conveying continuous, renewed occurrence (istimrar tajaddudi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 5:

﴿He was taught by one of mighty power﴾. That is, a mighty angel of great strength, and he is Jibril (peace be upon him), for he is the intermediary in the manifestation of extraordinary events (khawariq). And sufficient as evidence of the intensity of his strength is that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the black water that lies beneath the earth (al-thara), carried them on his wing, raised them up to the sky, then overturned them, and he cried out at Thamud with a single cry so that they became lifeless, prostrate. His descent upon the prophets and his ascent were faster than the blink of an eye (raj'at al-taraf).

Dhu Mirrah (ذُو مِرَّةٍ): that is, of sound judgment (ḥaṣāfah) in his intellect and opinion, and of firmness (matānah) in his religion.

Fa-istawā (فاسْتَوى): this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ʿallamahu (he taught him), by way of explanation (tafsīr), since it extends to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿what He revealed﴾. It explains the manner of the teaching; that is, he stood firm (istaqāma) in his true form in which Allah created him, not in the form in which he used to appear whenever he descended with the revelation. The reason is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to see him in the form in which he was created. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at Hira', and Jibril (peace be upon him) appeared to him from the east, filling the horizon from the west and covering the earth, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell down. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended in the form of a human being, embraced him, and began wiping the dust from his face.

It has been said: no prophet other than the Prophet (peace be upon him) saw him in his true form, for he saw him twice: once on earth and once in the heavens.

It has also been said: "istawā" means that he rose up by his strength to what he had been assigned of the command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verses 7–8:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while he was at the highest horizon﴾, that is, the horizon of the sun, is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "istawa" (he rose/appeared).

﴿Then he drew near﴾, that is, he intended to approach the Prophet, upon whom be the blessings and peace.

﴿And came down﴾, that is, he let himself hang down from the highest horizon while still attached to it, and so he drew near to the Prophet. It is said: "tadallat al-thamarah" (the fruit hung down), "dalla rijlayhi min al-sarir" (he let his legs dangle from the bed), and "adla dalwahu" (he lowered his bucket). Al-dawali (sing. dalwah) means the fruit hanging down.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verses 7–8:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while he was at the highest horizon﴾, that is, the horizon of the sun, is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "istawa" (he rose/appeared).

﴿Then he drew near﴾, that is, he intended to approach the Prophet, upon whom be the blessings and peace.

﴿And came down﴾, that is, he let himself hang down from the highest horizon while still attached to it, and so he drew near to the Prophet. It is said: "tadallat al-thamarah" (the fruit hung down), "dalla rijlayhi min al-sarir" (he let his legs dangle from the bed), and "adla dalwahu" (he lowered his bucket). Al-dawali (sing. dalwah) means the fruit hanging down.

﴿So he was﴾, meaning: the measure of the extent between them.

﴿Two bow-lengths away﴾, meaning: their measure. The words al-qāb (قَابَ), al-qīb (قِيبَ), al-qād (قَادَ), al-qayd (قَيْدَ) and al-qīs (قِيسَ) all mean "measure" (al-miqdār). It was also said that the one meant is Jibrīl (peace be upon him), as in your saying: "He is from me like the knot of the waistwrap (maʿqid al-izār)," meaning: he is very close to me.

﴿Or nearer﴾, meaning: according to your estimation, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿or even more﴾. The intended meaning is to depict the state of closeness (malakat al-ittiṣāl) and the certainty of his hearing what was revealed to him, by negating the misleading distance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 10:

﴿So He revealed﴾, i.e., Jibril (peace be upon him).

﴿to His servant﴾, the servant of Allah the Exalted. Its pronoun is mentioned before its antecedent because of how evident it is, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He left none upon its back﴾.

﴿what He revealed﴾, i.e., of the great matters for which expression is inadequate. Or: then Allah the Exalted revealed at that time, through the intermediary of Jibril, what He revealed. It has been said: He revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and forbidden to the nations until your community enters it.

The heart did not lie about what it saw.

That is: the heart (fu'ad) of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

"What it saw" means: what he saw with his eyes of the form of Jibril, peace be upon them both. That is, his heart did not say, regarding what he saw, "I do not recognize you." If it had said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him with his heart just as he saw him with his eyes.

It is also read "ma kadhdhaba" (did not deny), meaning: it affirmed him (sadaqahu) and did not doubt that it was Jibril in his form.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 12:

﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ That is: Will you deny him and then argue with him over what he sees with his own eyes? Or [is it] after what has been mentioned of his circumstances, which are incompatible with disputing? "Tumarunahu" (you dispute him) is from al-mira' (mira'), which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from maraa al-naqah (to milk the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants is milking what is in the other's possession. It is also recited as "Afatumrunahu" (afa-tumrūnahu), meaning: Will you overcome him in disputation, from mariytuhu, so I overpowered him (famaraytuhu)? And because of the sense of overpowering in it, it takes "ala" (over), as one says "ghalabtuhu 'ala kadhā" (I overcame him in such-and-such). It has also been said: "Afatumrunahu" means "Will you deny him?", from marraahu haqqahu (he denied his right) when he rejected it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 13:**

﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾. That is: by Allah, he certainly saw Jibril in his (true) form, another time, when descending. The word *nazlah* (descent) is put in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), which is a *marrah* (one occasion), because *fa'lah* is a noun denoting the single occurrence of the verb, so it takes the same ruling as it. It is also said: its implied sense is, "And he certainly saw him descending a descent, another (time)," so its accusative (*nasb*) is as a verbal noun (*masdar*).

﴿Near the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ It is a jujube tree (nabq) in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne ('Arsh). Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers that God Most High mentioned in His Book. A rider could travel in its shade for seventy years without crossing it. "Al-Muntaha" means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it lies at the furthest end of Paradise. It was also said: to it the knowledge and deeds of creation terminate, and no one knows what lies beyond it. It was also said: to it the souls of the martyrs ascend. It was also said: to it terminates what descends from above it and what ascends from below it.

It was said: the idafa (genitive construction) of "the lote-tree" to "al-Muntaha" is either the attribution of a thing to its place, as in your saying "the trees of the garden" (shajar al-bustan), or the attribution of a location to what is located in it, as in your saying "the book of jurisprudence" (kitab al-fiqh). The implied meaning is: a lote-tree beside which is the ultimate limit of the knowledge of creation. Or it is the attribution of possession to its owner, with the preposition and its object omitted, meaning: the lote-tree of the one to whom the ending belongs, who is God, Mighty and Majestic. God Most High said: ﴿To your Lord is the final destination﴾.

﴿Indeed near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾. That is, the Garden to which the God-fearing retreat, or the spirits of the martyrs. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). It has been said: the better view is that the circumstantial element is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) itself, and "Garden of Refuge" is raised by it as its agent (fā'iliyya).

The phrase of His, the Exalted: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covers it﴾ is an adverb of time (*zarf zaman*) modifying "he saw" (*ra'ah*), not the negative sentence that follows it, as some have said, because the negating *ma* (*ma al-nafiyya*) does not govern what precedes it. The verb *al-ghashayan* means covering and concealing, and from it comes *al-ghawashi* (coverings). It may also mean coming, as in the saying, "So-and-so visits me (*yaghshani*) every time," meaning he comes to me. The first meaning is the more fitting to the context. The vagueness of "that which covers" carries an evident magnification. Placing it after the object serves to arouse curiosity about it, meaning: He indeed saw him at the lote-tree at the time when it was covered by what cannot be comprehended by description nor fully expressed by explanation, in quality or in quantity. The use of the present tense (*al-mudari'*) is to narrate a past state (*hikayat al-hal al-madiyya*), bringing its wondrous image to mind, and to indicate the continuity of the covering through renewal. It has been said: a great multitude of angels cover it, worshipping God, the Exalted, there. It has been said: they visit it seeking blessing from it, as people visit the Ka'bah. It has been said: the rays (*sabahat*) of God's lights, may He be glorified and exalted, cover it when He manifests Himself to it, as He manifested Himself to the mountain, but it was stronger than the mountain and more steadfast, since it did not suffer what the mountain suffered of being crushed to dust. It has been said: a moth or locusts of gold cover it, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Dahhak. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I saw the lote-tree covered by a moth of gold, and I saw upon every leaf an angel standing, glorifying God, the Exalted." And from him, peace and blessings be upon him, comes: ﴿It is covered by a green canopy (*rafraf*) of birds﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 17:

﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ That is: the sight of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn away from what it saw.

﴿Nor did it transgress.﴾ Nor did it go beyond what it witnessed there of the wondrous and bewildering matters, which are beyond counting. Rather, he affirmed them with a true and certain affirmation. Or: he did not deviate from seeing the marvels he was commanded to see and was empowered to see, nor did he go beyond them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 18:

﴿He certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. That is: by Allah, he certainly saw the signs that are greatest and most magnificent, when he was taken up to the heavens. He was shown wonders of the dominion (al-mulk) and the realm of the unseen (al-malakut) that the scope of expression cannot encompass. It is also permissible that "al-kubra" (the greatest) be an adjective of "ayat" (signs), with the object omitted, meaning: something great of the signs of his Lord. It is also permissible that "min" (of) be superfluous (ziyada).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verses 19–20:

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ ﴿And Manat, the third, the other one?﴾ These are idols that they had. Al-Lat belonged to the Thaqif at al-Ta'if. It was said: it belonged to the Quraysh at Nakhla. It is of the pattern "fa'ala" from "lawa" (to turn around), because they used to turn around it and circumambulate it. It was also read with a doubled "t" (al-Latt), as an active participle by which a man became known, who used to knead ghee with oil and feed it to the pilgrims (p-158). It was also said: he used to knead sawiq (parched grain) with butter at al-Ta'if and feed it to the pilgrims; when he died, they devoted themselves at his grave, worshipping him. It was also said: he used to sit on a stone; when he died, the stone was named after him and was worshipped besides Allah. It was also said: the stone was in his likeness. Al-'Uzza is the feminine form of al-A'azz (the Mightiest). It belonged to the Ghatafan and was an acacia tree that they worshipped. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, who cut it down, and out of it came a female demon with loosened hair, placing her hand on her head and wailing. Khalid began striking her with the sword until he killed her. He informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "That was al-'Uzza, and she will never be worshipped again." Manat was a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuza'a. It was also said that it belonged to the Thaqif, and it seems she was named Manat because the blood of the sacrificial animals was poured out (tumna) near her, i.e., shed. It was read as "Mun'a'ah," which is of the pattern "maf'ala" from "al-naw'" (the rising of a star/rain-star), as if they sought rain near her through the risings of the stars, seeking blessing by her. Al-Ukhra (the other one) is an epithet of disparagement for her, meaning the late-coming, of low rank. It is also permissible that the priority and precedence among them belonged to al-Lat and al-'Uzza. Moreover, along with their worship of these, they used to say: the angels and those idols are the daughters of Allah, exalted is Allah far above that, greatly exalted. So it was said to them in rebuke and reproach: ﴿Have you considered?﴾ ...etc. The interrogative hamza is for denial, and the fa' is for directing it toward the sequence of the vision upon what was mentioned of the affairs of Allah the Exalted, which are utterly incompatible with them. The verb is of the heart (qalbiyya), and its second object is omitted, due to the indication of the situation. The meaning: following what you have heard of the signs of the perfection of Allah's greatness in His dominion, His sovereignty, His majesty, His might, the perfection of His power and the effectiveness of His command, in the exalted assembly, under the earth, and between them, did you see these idols, despite their utter lowliness and insignificance, as daughters of Allah the Exalted? It was also said: the meaning is: did you see these idols, despite their lowliness and humiliation, as partners of Allah the Exalted, along with what preceded of His greatness? It was also said: tell me about your gods, do they have any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might was described in the preceding verses? It was also said: the meaning is: did you suppose that these idols you worship benefit you? It was also said: did you suppose that they will intercede for you in the Hereafter? It was also said: consider these idols: if you worship them they will not benefit you, and if you abandon them they will not harm you. The first is the truth, as His saying the Exalted attests:

﴿Is the male for you, and for Him the female?﴾ This is a clear testimony, for it is a reproach built upon the first reproach. Since its basis is preferring their own side over His exalted side, by attributing to Him, exalted is He, females while choosing males for themselves, the ground (manat) of the first reproach must be that very attribution, so that the second reproach can be built upon it. It is evident that none of the interpretations mentioned above contains any trace or mark of that attribution.

As for what has been said, that this clause is a second object (maf'ul thani) of "seeing" (al-ru'yah), and that it is free of a returning pronoun to the first object, because the original would be: "Tell me: that al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, is the male for you and for Him they are," meaning those idols, and that it was placed in the position of "the female" for the sake of observing the verse endings (al-fawasil) and realizing the ground of the rebuke: along with what it contains of far-fetched explanations (tamahhulat), from which the sanctity of the Revelation should be cleared, it requires restricting the rebuke to preferring their base side over the mighty, glorious side of God, without addressing the rebuke over the attribution of offspring to Him, glorified is He.

﴿Such⁠﴾ refers to the division implied by the interrogative sentence.

﴿Then that is an unjust division﴾, meaning: unjust, since you assign to Him, exalted is He, what you yourselves dislike (p-159) for yourselves. It is fu'là (a pattern) from al-ḍayz, which means injustice, but its first letter was given a kasra so that the yā' would be preserved, as was done in "bīḍ" (white); for fu'lā with a kasra does not occur as an adjective. It is also read "ḍi'zā" with a hamza, from ḍa'aza-hu, meaning he wronged him, taken as a verbal noun (maṣdar) described by it. It is also read "ḍayzā", either as a maṣdar described by it, like da'wā (claim), or as an adjective, like sakrā (drunk) and 'aṭshā (thirsty).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 23:

﴿It is not but﴾: the pronoun refers to the idols, i.e., the idols, in respect of the divinity which they claim.

﴿Nothing but names﴾: pure names, with nothing whatsoever beneath them of what they indicate in terms of the meaning of divinity. The words of the Exalted, ﴿which you have named﴾, are an attribute of "names," and its pronoun refers to them, not to the idols. The meaning is: you have made them names, not you have made names for them. For tasmiyah (naming) is a relation between the name (ism) and the named (musamma). When it is considered in relation to the name, its meaning is making it a name for the named; and if it is considered in relation to the named, its meaning is making it named by the name. The first meaning was chosen here, without addressing the named, in order to establish that those idols which they call gods are bare names with no named referents at all, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿You do not worship besides Him except names which you have named﴾, etc., not that there are named referents but they do not deserve the naming. And it was said: the pronoun refers to the three names mentioned, since they used to apply them to those idols, believing that they deserve devotion, veneration, and approach through offerings.

And you are aware that even if it is granted that the mentioned names indicate the establishment of those particular meanings for the idols, there is no further benefit in negating them from them; rather, the purpose is the negation of divinity from them, as is their well-known claim concerning all idols, in a demonstrative manner, for the negation of the qualified entails the negation of the quality by way of greater priority. That is: they are merely names devoid of named referents, which you have coined.

﴿You and your fathers﴾: in accordance with your vain desires.

﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾: no proof upon which you rely.

﴿They follow only﴾: a shift to the third person, signifying that enumerating their abominations required turning away from them and relating their crimes to others. That is: they follow, in what has been mentioned of naming and acting upon its consequences, nothing.

﴿but conjecture﴾: but the mere imagining that what they hold to be true is true, a false imagining.

﴿and what the souls desire﴾: that is, what their commanding-to-evil souls (nafs ammarah bi-l-su') desire.

﴿Yet guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾: it was said: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "they follow," or a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). Whichever it is, it contains emphasis on the nullity of following conjecture, which is the self, and an increase in the reproach of their condition, for following these two is abominable from any person whatsoever, and from one whom God the Exalted has guided by sending the Messenger ﷺ and sending down the Book, it is even more abominable.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 24:

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ "Am" (أمْ) is disjunctive (munqati'a), and what is in it of "bal" (بَلْ, "rather/nay") is for transition from explaining that what they hold to is supported only by their delusion and their souls' desires, to explaining that this is something that brings no benefit at all. The hamza is for denunciation and negation, meaning: man does not have everything that he wishes and that his soul desires, from among the matters of which their empty hopes of intercession from the gods and their like are a part, which scarcely enter into existence.

﴿So to Allah belongs the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ This is a justification for the negation that a human being should have whatever he wishes as of right, for the exclusive ownership of all the affairs of the Hereafter and the first life by Him, exalted is He, necessitates that no affair whatsoever belongs to anyone else.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 26:

And His saying, ﴿And how many an angel there is in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing﴾ is a despairing of them (the polytheists) from what they had attached their hopes to, namely the intercession of the angels for them, and it entails their despair of the intercession of the idols by way of a fortiori reasoning (bi-tariq al-awlawiyyah). "Kam" (how many) here is khabariyyah (declarative), conveying multiplicity; its position is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the negated clause. The pronoun in "shafa'atuhum" (their intercession) is plural while "malak" (angel) is singular, taking into account the meaning: i.e., many of the angels, their intercession with Allah Most High will avail nothing whatsoever, at any time.

﴿Except after Allah gives permission﴾ to them to intercede,

﴿for whom He wills﴾ that they should intercede for him,

﴿and approves﴾ and sees him as worthy of intercession from among the people of tawhid (monotheism) and faith. As for those other than them from among the people of disbelief and transgression, they are far removed from the permission of Allah Most High, and (they are far removed) from intercession by a thousand degrees. So if the state of the angels regarding intercession is as mentioned, then what do you suppose the state of the idols is?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ and in what it contains of punishment for what they engage in of disbelief and sins.

﴿They name the angels﴾, who are exalted above every attribute of deficiency absolutely, ﴿with the name of females﴾. They name each one of them [with a feminine name], for their saying "the angels are the daughters of Allah" is a declaration on their part that each of them is His daughter, exalted is He, and this is the naming with the feminine. Connecting this [naming] to not believing in the Hereafter indicates that it is so monstrous and grievous, and that it entails punishment in the Hereafter, such that none would dare to commit it except one who does not believe in it at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 28:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "yusammuna" (they name). That is, they name it, while the circumstance is that they have no knowledge at all of what they are saying. It has also been read as "bihā" (with it), i.e., with the angels, or with the naming (al-tasmiya).

﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ in that matter.

﴿And conjecture﴾ — the false conjecture.

﴿Indeed, conjecture﴾ — i.e., the category of conjecture, as indicated by the use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun.

﴿Avails nothing against the truth﴾ — from "ighna" (to avail). For the truth, which is an expression for the reality of a thing, is not attained except by knowledge, and conjecture carries no weight in matters of real cognition. It is only taken into account in practical matters (al-'amaliyyat, i.e., practical rulings) and what leads to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 29:

﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our Reminder﴾ That is: from them. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the place of their pronoun serves to make their description by the ugly attributes contained in its clause (silah) a means of establishing the ruling on them. That is: turn away from those who have turned away from Our Reminder, which yields certain knowledge, namely the Qur'an, which encompasses the sciences of the earlier and later generations and which reminds of the matters of the Hereafter; or [it means] turn away from Our Reminder as it ought to be received, for that entails remembrance of the Hereafter and the matters in it that are desired and those from which one flees.

﴿And he desires nothing but the life of this world﴾ contented with it, confining his outlook to it. The intended meaning is the prohibition of calling him to the truth and of paying attention to his affair. He said: whoever has turned away from what has been mentioned and has immersed himself in this world, such that it is the limit of his aspiration and the utmost of his striving, the call to its opposite increases him only in obstinacy and persistence in falsehood. (p-161)

Translation:

﴿That﴾ means: what led them to the state they are in, of turning away and limiting their aspiration to the life of this world.

﴿Their knowledge extends no further﴾ — they scarcely go beyond it to anything else, until admonition and guidance benefit them. The pronoun in "mablaghuhum" is plural in consideration of the meaning of "man" (whoever), just as its singular form earlier was in consideration of its wording. By "knowledge" is meant mere perception, encompassing corrupt conjecture. The clause is a parenthetical statement confirming the content of what precedes it, namely the limiting of aspiration to the life of this world. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾, it is the reason for the command to turn away. The repetition of ﴿He is most knowing﴾ serves to increase the affirmation and to signal the complete disparity between the two known groups. By "who strays" is meant one who persists in it and never returns to guidance at all; by "who is guided" is meant one whose nature is to be guided in general. That is: He is the one who has perfect knowledge of those who never desist from error ever, and of those who accept guidance in general, and none other. So do not tire yourself out in calling them, for they belong to the first category. In the explanation of the command to turn away, by stating that the knowledge of the conditions of both groups is restricted to Him, the peace be upon him is relieved of concern for their affairs, and this is an allusion to the fact that He, the Exalted, treats them in accordance with His knowledge of them, rewarding each of them with the recompense that befits them. Thus there is in it an implicit threat and promise, as will be stated explicitly later.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 31:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ meaning: by creation and ownership, not belonging to anyone else at all, neither independently nor in partnership. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that He may recompense﴾ ...etc. is connected to what is indicated by "He knows best" ...etc., and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it, for the fact that all things are created by Him, exalted is He, is among what confirms His knowledge of their states, "Does He not know who created?" It is as if it were said: He knows the misguidance of those who go astray and the guidance of those who are guided, and He preserves both, ﴿so that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾, meaning: with the punishment for what they did of misguidance, which He expressed as "evil" to clarify its state, or because of what they did.

﴿And recompense those who did good﴾, meaning: those who were guided.

﴿With the best [reward]﴾, meaning: with the best reward, which is Paradise, or because of their good deeds. It has been said that it is connected to what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, as if it were said: He created what is in them so that He may recompense ...etc. It has also been said that it is connected to "went astray" and "was guided," with the lam being of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), meaning: He knows best who has gone astray, so that his affair may end with Allah recompensing him for his deed, and who has been guided, so that his affair may end with Him recompensing him with the best. There is in this a remoteness that is not hidden. And the repetition of the verb is to show the complete concern with the matter of recompense and to draw attention to the difference between the two recompenses.

(p-162) ﴿The ones who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ith m)﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the second relative pronoun (al-mawsul al-thani). The use of the imperfect tense in its relative clause indicates the renewal and continuity of avoidance. Alternatively, it is an explanatory apposition (bayan), or a qualifying adjective (na't), or it is in the accusative by way of praise (mansub 'ala al-madh). "Kaba'ir al-ithm" means the sins whose punishment is great, that is, those for which a specific threat (wa'id) has been prescribed. It is also read as "kabir al-ithm," meaning the category (jins) or shirk.

﴿and the indecencies (fawahish)﴾: that is, what is especially gross among the major sins.

﴿except for minor lapses (al-lamam)﴾: that is, except what is small and slight, for it is forgiven for one who avoids the major sins. It has been said that it refers to a glance, a wink, or a kiss. It has also been said that it is a passing thought of sin. And it has been said that it is every sin for which God has not prescribed a legal penalty (hadd) or a punishment ('adhab). It has also been said that it is the habit of the soul, now and then. The exception is disjunctive (munqati').

﴿Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness (wasi' al-maghfirah)﴾, in that He forgives minor sins for those who avoid major sins. The sentence is therefore a justification (ta'lil) for the exception of minor lapses and an alert (tanbih) that their exclusion from the ruling of accountability is not because they are free of sin in themselves, but because of the vastness of the divine forgiveness. It has been said that the meaning is: He has the right to forgive whom He wills among the believers whatever sins He wills, small or great. Perhaps the reason that the promise to the evildoers and the promise to the good-doers is followed by this statement is so that the one who has committed a major sin does not despair of His mercy, and does not imagine that punishment is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He.

﴿He knows you best (huwa a'lamu bikum)﴾: that is, He knows your conditions.

﴿when He produced you (idh ansha'akum)﴾: within the production of your father Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿from the earth (min al-ard)﴾: a general production, as has been explained repeatedly before.

﴿And when you were embryos (wa-idh antum ajinnah)﴾: that is, at the time you were embryos.

﴿in the wombs of your mothers (fi buṭun ummahatikum)﴾: in various stages arranged in sequence, none of which is hidden from Him, of any of your conditions and any of your deeds, among which is the minor lapse, whose consequence would have befallen you were it not for the vast forgiveness. The sentence is therefore a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what preceded it. The fa' in His statement, ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves (fa-la tuzakku anfusakum)﴾, indicates the sequence of the prohibition against self-praise upon what has preceded: that the non-accountability for minor lapses is not because they are not of the category of sins, but purely because of His forgiveness, while He knows they proceed from you. That is: since the matter is as it is, do not praise yourselves for being entirely free of sins, or for what entails it of the purity of deeds and the growth of good, but rather thank God for His grace and His forgiveness.

﴿He knows best who has been mindful of God (huwa a'lamu bimani ittaqa)﴾ against all sins. This is a resumptive clause confirming the prohibition, and it indicates that among people there are those who guard against them entirely. It has been said: some people used to do good deeds and then say, "our prayer, our fasting, and our pilgrimage," so this was revealed. This applies when it is done out of self-admiration or showing off. As for one who believes that the good deeds he performs are from God, by His success and His support, and who does not intend by them to seek praise, he is not among those who purify themselves, for delight in obedience is itself obedience and mentioning it is gratitude.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 33:

﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is: away from following the truth and holding firm to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 34:

﴿And he gave a little﴾, i.e., something little, or a little giving.

﴿And ceased﴾, i.e., he cut off the giving, (p-163) from their saying: akdā al-hāfir (the digger "ceased"), when he reached the kudya (a hard rock-like stratum), so he cannot dig further. They said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He used to follow the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some of the polytheists reproached him and said to him: "You have abandoned the religion of the elders and misled them." He said: "I fear the punishment of Allah." So they guaranteed that they would bear the punishment on his behalf if he gave them some of his wealth. He apostatized and gave them part of what was agreed, but withheld the rest.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, when he would agree with the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) in some matters.

It was also said: concerning Abu Jahl, who would sometimes agree with the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) in some matters, and would say: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands us to noble character." This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he gave a little and ceased﴾. The first view is the most well-known and fits what follows it in His saying, exalted is He:
﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ ...etc. That is: does he have knowledge of the unseen matters, among which is his companion bearing his burden on the Day of Resurrection?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verses 36–37:

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses,﴾ ﴿and of Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]?﴾ That is, he fully performed and completed what he was tested with of the words, or what he was commanded with, or he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he pledged to God. His being singled out for this is because he bore what no one else could bear, such as patience over the fire of Nimrod (Numrud), until, when he was thrown into the fire, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and said, "Do you have any need?" He replied, "As for you, no." Also [he was singled out for bearing] the sacrifice of his son. It is also related that he would walk one farsakh (a unit of distance, about three miles) every day in search of a guest. If he found one, he honored him; otherwise he intended to fast. The mention of Moses first is because his scrolls, which are the Torah, are better known and more numerous among them (the Jews).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verses 36–37:

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses,﴾ ﴿and of Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]?﴾ That is, he fully performed and completed what he was tested with of the words, or what he was commanded with, or he went to great lengths in fulfilling what he pledged to God. His being singled out for this is because he bore what no one else could bear, such as patience over the fire of Nimrod (Numrud), until, when he was thrown into the fire, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and said, "Do you have any need?" He replied, "As for you, no." Also [he was singled out for bearing] the sacrifice of his son. It is also related that he would walk one farsakh (a unit of distance, about three miles) every day in search of a guest. If he found one, he honored him; otherwise he intended to fast. The mention of Moses first is because his scrolls, which are the Torah, are better known and more numerous among them (the Jews).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 38:

﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another⦆ That is: no soul whose nature is to bear burdens shall bear the burden of another soul. This is on the reading that "an" (أنْ) is the lightened form of the heavy "anna" (المُخَفَّفَةُ مِنَ الثَّقِيلَةِ), with its pronoun of matter (ضمير الشأن, the implicit subject of the sentence) omitted, and the negated clause serving as its predicate. The clause has a place in the grammatical case of the genitive (الجَرُّ) as an apposition (بَدَلٌ) to what is in the scrolls of Musa, or in the nominative (الرَّفْعِ) as the predicate of an omitted subject, as though it were said: "What is in their scrolls?" And it was said: "It is that no bearer of burdens..." and so on.

The meaning is: no one is held to account for the sin of another, so that the second person may be freed from his punishment. Nor does his saying, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection⦆ detract from this, for that is the burden of misguidance (وِزْرُ الإضْلالِ), which is his own burden.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾ is an explanation of the fact that a person does not benefit from the deeds of another in terms of bringing benefit to himself, following the explanation of his not benefiting from them in terms of averting harm from himself. As for the intercession (shafa'ah) of the Prophets, peace be upon them, the seeking of forgiveness (istighfar) by the angels, peace be upon them, the supplication (du'a') of the living for the dead, their giving of charity on their behalf, and other things that cannot be counted, of the beneficial matters for a person, although they are certainly not from his own deeds, nevertheless, since the basis of the benefit of each of them is his deed, which is faith and righteousness, and none of them has any benefit without it, the beneficial thing is made to be his very deed, even if it is by the joining of another's deed to it. "And that" (wa-an) is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) like its sister, conjoined to what precedes it, and likewise His saying, Exalted is He:

"And that his striving will be seen" (Q. 53:40). That is: it will be presented to him and disclosed to him on the Day of Resurrection in his record and in his scale, from "I showed him (araytuhu) the thing."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 41:

﴿Then he will be recompensed for it﴾ That is: a person is recompensed for his effort (sa'y). One says: "Allah recompensed him for his deed" (jazahu Allahu bi-'amalihi), and "recompensed him for his deed" (jazahu 'ala 'amalihi), and "recompensed him his deed" (jazahu 'amalahu), by dropping the preposition and making the verb reach its object directly. It is permissible to make the pronoun refer to "the recompense" (al-jaza'), then it is explained by His words, exalted is He: ﴿the fullest recompense﴾; or the pronoun may be made a substitute (badal) for it, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they secretly conferred, those who did wrong﴾.

And that to your Lord is the finality (al-muntaha, the ultimate end): that is, the ending of creation and their return to Him, exalted is He, and not to anyone else, either independently or in partnership. It is also read with the "inna" (indeed) pronounced with a kasra, as a new sentence (ibtida', beginning).

And that He it is who makes [people] laugh and weep. ... 

Let me restate precisely per the instructions.

﴿And that it is He who makes [people] laugh and makes [them] weep﴾ — that is: He is the One who created the two faculties of laughing and weeping.

Translation:

﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life.﴾ None other than Him is able to cause death and give life, for the effect of the killer is only the dismantling of the structure and the severing of connection; death occurs at his hand only through God's act, according to custom (al-'adah).

And that He created the two mates, the male and the female, from a drop of semen when it is emitted (﴿وَأنَّهُ خَلَقَ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ والأُنْثى﴾ "And that He created the two mates, the male and the female," ﴿مِن نُطْفَةٍ إذا تُمْنى﴾ "from a drop of semen when it is emitted"), [the drop] that gushes into the womb; or it is created [or formed]; or the child is determined from it, from the seminal fluid (maniyy), in the sense of "qaddara" (to decree or determine).

And that He created the two mates, the male and the female, from a drop of semen when it is emitted (﴿وَأنَّهُ خَلَقَ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ والأُنْثى﴾ "And that He created the two mates, the male and the female," ﴿مِن نُطْفَةٍ إذا تُمْنى﴾ "from a drop of semen when it is emitted"), [the drop] that gushes into the womb; or it is created [or formed]; or the child is determined from it, from the seminal fluid (maniyy), in the sense of "qaddara" (to decree or determine).

Verse 47 of Surah al-Najm (53): ﴿And that upon Him is the final creation (al-nash'ah al-ukhra)﴾. That is: the bringing back to life after death, fulfilling His promise. It is also read as "al-nash'a'ah" with a long vowel (al-madd), and this too is a verbal noun (masdar) of nasha'ahu.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 48:

﴿And that He is the One Who enriches and grants possessions.﴾ "Wa-aqna" means He bestowed qinya (property, i.e. wealth that is acquired and preserved), which is wealth that is accumulated and kept. He singled it out for mention because it is the most noble of wealth, or the most pleasing. Its realization is that He makes contentment (ridha) a qinya for him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 49:

﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius.﴾ That is, the Lord of their deity. It is al-'Abur (Sirius), and it is brighter in light than al-Ghumaysa', and Khuza'ah used to worship it. A man from their nobles, Abu Kabsha, established this practice for them. Quraysh used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Abu Kabsha," likening him to him, peace and blessings be upon him, because he opposed them in their religion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 50:

﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾ (p-165) They are the people of Hud, peace be upon him, and the second ʿAd is Iram. It is also said: the "first" refers to the ancient ones, because they were the first nation to be destroyed after the people of Noah. The reading "ʿAdun al-ūlā" is also transmitted, with the hamza elided and its vowel transferred to the lam; and "ʿAdun lūlā" is transmitted, with the tanwin assimilated into the lam, the hamza of ūlā dropped, and its vowel transferred to the lam of the definite article.

And Thamud (﴿وَثَمُودَ﴾): it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ʿĀd, because what follows it is not governed by what precedes it (the following verb does not act upon it). It is also read as "wa-Thamūdan" with tanwin.

﴿فَما أبْقى﴾: that is, He left none of the two groups (al-farīqayn) remaining.

"And the people of Noah before them" is coordinated with it as well.

"From before" means: from before the destruction of 'Ad and Thamud.

"Indeed they were more wrongdoing and more rebellious" than the two groups, since they used to harm him, turn people away from him, and warn their children not to listen to him. They would beat him, peace be upon him, until there was no movement left in him, and his supplication had no effect on them for nearly a thousand years.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 53:

﴿Wal-Mu'tafikah﴾ (And the overturned cities) are the towns of the people of Lut (Lot), which were overturned with their inhabitants, i.e., turned upside down with them.

﴿Ahwa﴾ (He cast down): i.e., He brought them down to the earth after raising them on the wing of Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, up to the sky.
Then there covered them ﴿that which covered them﴾, of the various kinds of punishment. In it is such terror and dreadfulness that nothing lies beyond it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 55:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ "Tatamara" means "tatashakkaku" (you doubt). The address is to the Messenger, peace be upon him, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾, or it is addressed to every person. The attribution of the act of disputing (tamari) to a single addressee is in consideration of its multiplicity according to the multiplicity of its object (mute'allaq). For the form of reciprocity (sigha al-tafa'ul), although it is coined to indicate that the act proceeds from multiple parties and falls upon them in such a way that each of them is both agent and object together, it may nonetheless be stripped of the second meaning, so that only the first meaning is intended, as in "yatada'unahum" (they call them), i.e., "yad'unahum." It may also be stripped of that as well, so that the act is considered multiple merely by the multiplicity of its object, as is the case in what we are discussing, for the disputing is multiple according to the multiplicity of the favours. So reflect. As for calling the enumerated matters "favours" (ala') even though some of them are retributions (niqam), it is because they are also blessings (ni'am) in that they are a victory for the prophets and the believers and a vengeance on their behalf, and in them are admonitions (i'zat) and lessons ('ibar) for those who take heed.

This is a Qur'anic quotation: ﴿This is a warner from the warnings of old﴾. "Hadha" (this) is either a reference to the Qur'an, and "nadhir" (warner) is then a verbal noun (masdar), or it refers to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and "nadhir" then carries the sense of "mundhir" (one who warns). Whichever is the case, the tanwin (nunation) on "nadhir" is for emphasis (tafkhim), and "min" (from) is connected to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier (na't) for "nadhir", confirming it and carrying a threat. That is: this Qur'an which you are witnessing is a warner of the same kind as the earlier warnings whose outcome you have heard; or, this Messenger is a warner of the same class as the first warners. The plural "al-ula" (the first) is used in the sense of the group (ta'wil al-jama'ah) in consideration of the rhyme endings (fawasil), and you have known the circumstances of their people who were warned. And in its sequence with the words of the Exalted:

Qur'an 53:57 – "The imminent one has drawn near."

It is an indication that their punishment is deferred until the Day of Resurrection; that is, the Hour, described as drawing near, has come close, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ (54:1).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 58:

﴿There is none to disclose it besides Allah﴾. That is: there is no soul able to disclose it when it occurs except Allah, the Exalted, yet He does not disclose it; or, there is now no soul that can postpone it except Allah, the Exalted, for He is the one who delays it; or, there is no one to disclose it at its appointed time except Allah, the Exalted, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿None but He will manifest it at its time﴾. Or: there is no disclosure from other than Allah, the Exalted, with the understanding that kashifah (disclosure) is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-'afiyah (well-being).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 53, verse 59:**

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾ That is: the Qur'an.

﴿Do you wonder﴾ in denial (inkaran).

**Verse 53:60:** ﴿And you laugh⁠﻿ in mockery,⁠﻿ while it is furthest of all things from such⁠﻿ (a matter)﻿﴾ — [the commentary's wording: "استهزاءً مع كونه أبعد شيء من ذلك"].

Translation of the commentary:

"﴿And you laugh﴾ in mockery, while it is the furthest thing from that (i.e., from what befits such a matter)."

"﴿And do not weep﴾ out of grief over what you neglected concerning its affair, and out of fear that there may befall you what befell the nations mentioned."

"And you are proud/heedless" — "﴿And you are sāmidūn﴾" meaning: heedless (lāhūn) or proud (mustakbirūn), from samada the camel, when it raised its head; or singers (mughannūn), so that you distract people from listening to it, from al-sumūd in the sense of singing, according to the dialect of Ḥimyar; or humbled and still (khāshi'ūn jāmidūn), from al-sumūd in the sense of stillness and humility, as in the words of one who said:

"Misfortunes (al-ḥidthān) cast at the women of the house of Sa'd with a decree, so they prostrated themselves to it, lowering their heads (samadna lahu sujūdan)

So he turned their black hair white, and turned their white faces black."

The clause is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "lā tabkūn" (you do not weep), except that its content, on the last interpretation, is a restriction on the negated element, and the rebuke falls on the negation of both weeping and sumūd together; on the earlier interpretations, it is a restriction on the negation, and the rebuke is directed at the negation of weeping while sumūd exists. The first is more fitting to the requirement of the context, so reflect upon it.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So prostrate to God and worship [Him]﴾, is for the sequencing of the command, or for what necessitates it, in light of what has been established regarding the falsehood of confronting the Qur'an with denial and mockery, and the obligation of receiving it with faith, together with complete humility and submissiveness. That is: since the matter is as such, then prostrate to God, who sent it down, and worship [Him].

From the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "Whoever recites Surat al-Najm, God, exalted is He, will grant him ten good deeds for each number of those who believed in Muhammad and those who denied him in Mecca, may God ennoble it."
